newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Uganda denies its troops are fighting in Zaire.
newsitem.headline: Uganda denies its troops are fighting in Zaire.

text.p: Uganda denied on Friday French accusations Ugandan troops were fighting in eastern Zaire where rebels vowed to seize the northeast capital of Kisangani very soon.
Hope Kivengere, spokeswoman for Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni, told Reuters that Uganda had no troops in eastern Zaire and the French allegations were "ridiculous and strange".

French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette told a newspaper on Thursday: "What must stop are the interventions of its (Zaire's) neighbours, particularly Uganda whose activity on Zairean soil is an established fact."
But de Charette indicated France, seeking U.N. intervention to stop hostilities in a move that could save President Mobutu Sese Seko's authority, would not intervene alone in Zaire.
Kivengere challenged France to provide proof of the alleged Ugandan involvement in the five-month-old war. Museveni denied on a visit to Paris last month there were any Ugandan troops in Zaire.
Zaire has also accused Uganda, Rwanda and Burundi of sending troops to back the rebels, who have captured much of eastern Zaire. The three countries and rebels denied the accusations.

In the rebel headquarters in the city Goma on the border with Rwanda, rebel foreign affairs chief Bizima Karaha said the rebels would not agree to a ceasefire before direct negotiations as demanded by Kinshasa by its agreeing to a U.N. peace plan.
"The crumbling Kinshasa government...asked for a ceasefire as it is weak militarily. They want to save what is left, they know Kisangani will fall very soon," he told a news conference on Thursday.
Karaha said rebel forces killed 114 Zairean troops at Panga village, 200 km (120 miles) northeast of Kisangani, and rebel forces were 10 km (six miles) from Kisangani and its airport.
Kisangani, the northeast capital, and its airport were the base for a government counter-offensive that failed to halt rebel advances. Zairean army officers say they are preparing to defend the city.
The rebels hope its fall will force Mobutu, 66, who seized power in Zaire in 1965 and is now in Europe where he had surgery for prostate cancer last August, to negotiate with them and stand down.

Rebels have taken a stretch of the east 1,000 km (600 miles) long bordering on Sudan, Uganda, Rwanda, Burundi and Tanzania since October. Efforts by foreign mercenaries to bolster the army failed because of poor logistics, training and low morale.
Residents of the east say popular support for the rebels is growing, especially in areas looted by Zairean troops who usually melt away with their booty before the rebels arrive.
Reports from the southern mining province of Shaba pointed on Thursday for the first time to a groundswell of support for the guerrillas in at least parts of the separatist region.
Local Zaireans in the town of Manono deep in the copper-rich province declared it "rebel-held territory" at a rally on Monday after a scuffle with gendarmes, three sources in the region told Reuters.
The defence ministry and state Zairean radio denied the town had fallen. Rebel leader Laurent Kabila said his forces took Manono on Monday but it is unclear whether his guerrillas were there.
